result:
The city had a lost-and-found office for sounds.

It occupied a narrow room beneath the railway station, between a locksmith and a shop that had been “Opening Soon” for eleven years. Most people walked past without noticing it. Those who entered generally stood in the doorway for a moment, listening.

Behind the counter, a woman named Mara kept the sounds in small wooden drawers.

Rain on a childhood roof. A particular laugh. The click of a kitchen light switched on by someone who no longer lived there.

There were ordinary things, too. Misplaced ringtones. The second half of a sentence drowned out by a passing truck. One drawer contained nothing but a man saying, “Actually, never mind.”

One Thursday, a boy arrived carrying an empty jam jar.

“I found this,” he said.

Mara took the jar and held it to her ear.

Inside was the soft scrape of a chair being pulled closer to another chair.

“Where?”

“At our house. After dinner.”

“Does someone need it back?”

The boy considered this.

“I think we need more of it.”

Mara looked at him over her glasses. Then she stood, turned the sign on the door to CLOSED, and took two chairs from the little table beside the window.

She set them side by side.

“Leave the lid off,” she said.

They sat watching travelers cross the station steps. After a while, the boy began to tell her about dinner: the burnt potatoes, his father’s new haircut, the unfairness of having to wash a pan he hadn’t used.

Mara listened. When he paused, she pulled her chair a little closer.

The boy glanced at the jar.

“Will that one stay in there?”

“Some of it.”

He left before five, carrying the jar carefully in both hands.

Mara put her chair back beside the table. She left the other one where it was.
